name: How accurate is a square-foot construction cost estimate?

mainEntity.name: When is square-foot pricing accurate enough, and when does it become misleading?
mainEntity.text: When is square-foot pricing accurate enough, and when does it become misleading?

acceptedAnswer.text: Square-foot pricing is a practical starting point, but it is only accurate when the project is fairly standard and the finish level is already known. It becomes unreliable when the job includes hillside grading, basement excavation, major structural changes, premium materials, or complex mechanical systems. In Los Angeles, two homes with the same square footage can have very different budgets because access, foundation work, and finish quality change the cost far more than size alone. A good square-foot estimate is best used to test feasibility in the early stage. Once the design gets serious, the estimate should shift to a detailed takeoff with separate pricing for labor, materials, permits, and contingency. That approach is much more useful for owners in Glendale, Pasadena, Burbank, and North Hollywood who need a budget that can survive design development and permit review.
acceptedAnswer.description: Square-foot pricing is useful for early budgeting, but it becomes misleading when the project has unusual site conditions, custom finishes, complex structure, or major MEP upgrades. It works best as a rough planning tool, not as a final bid, because local labor, access, and code requirements can change the real cost.
